opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like some big, dramatic decision. It felt more like I was following what I was curious about. Looking back, it was clearly a departure from the path most people around me were on, but in the moment I was just thinking, "This is the thing I actually want to spend my days doing."

There was definitely some anxiety. When you step off the standard track, you lose the built-in signals that tell you you're doing okay: the exams, the rankings, the clear next step. You have to build your own sense of progress, and some days you wonder whether you've made a huge mistake. My family had questions too, which is natural. They wanted to know there was a plan.

What helped was realizing that the mainstream path is just one way of organizing learning. It works well for many people, but it isn't the only route to doing meaningful work. I learned a lot by building things, getting stuck, and figuring out how to get unstuck, often more than I would have by optimizing for a test. That habit of teaching yourself and being comfortable with not knowing turned out to matter a lot later, especially in research, where nobody hands you the answer.

So my feelings were mixed: a little uncertain and a little scared, but mostly excited. I don't think I'd tell everyone to do what I did. I would tell people it's okay to take your curiosity seriously, even if it leads somewhere less conventional.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the departure did not feel like a big or dramatic decision at the time and describes mixed anxiety and excitement. It does not convey that Danfei viewed it as impressive.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like some bold, dramatic decision. It felt more like I was just following my curiosity and the path kind of bent on its own. I grew up in a pretty traditional system where there's one track everyone's supposed to be on, and I remember noticing early that the things I actually wanted to spend my time on, tinkering, building things, trying to make machines do something, didn't really fit neatly into that track.

So there was definitely some anxiety. You see your friends doing the "right" thing, and you wonder if you're making a mistake you won't be able to undo. My family was supportive, but I think they were also a little nervous, and I felt that. There were a lot of nights where I was asking myself, am I being brave or am I just being stubborn?

But what I kept coming back to was that the conventional path felt like optimizing for a scoreboard someone else had designed. And I cared more about whether I was learning things that actually mattered to me. Once I framed it that way, it got easier. Not easy, but easier. I think that mindset ended up being really useful later in research too, because research is basically a long series of departures from what everyone else is doing, and you have to get comfortable with that discomfort.

Looking back, I'm grateful I did it when the stakes were relatively low. It taught me that the fear of leaving the mainstream is usually much bigger than the actual cost of it.

r001.rationale: He says it did not feel like a bold, dramatic decision at the time; he describes curiosity and anxiety instead of viewing it as impressive.

astra-6.text: It was a mix of excitement and uncertainty. Mainstream education gives you a clear path, and stepping away from that means you have to figure out what matters to you and how you want to learn. There was a sense of freedom, but also that question of, “Am I making the right decision?” I didn’t have everything figured out.
